title: Some Kind of Mettle
subtitle: The find at Sutter's Mill and the California gold rush, Coloma, San Francisco and the diggings, 1848–1852
intro: On a Monday in January 1848 a Mormon labourer on a half-built sawmill in the Sierra foothills wrote one line in his diary: some kind of metal had turned up in the tail race, and it looked like gold. Within a year the President of the United States had confirmed the find to Congress. Within two, a hundred thousand newcomers were in California, the territory had become a state, and the people whose land it was were being killed, indentured and starved off it.

This chapter sets the find and the rush side by side through people who stood in very different places. On the mill crew are Henry Bigler and Azariah Smith, wage hands who wanted only enough money to rejoin their families. The owner is John Sutter, whose fort and Native workforce dissolved in months. Then come the San Francisco weeklies that first shrugged and then folded; Walter Colton, magistrate of an emptying capital; Colonel Mason, who rode out to count; and President Polk, who made it official.

The rush was never only an American story. Antonio Franco Coronel, a Californio from Los Angeles, and Vicente Pérez Rosales, a Chilean, struck gold early and were driven off their claims as 'foreigners' in 1849. Norman Asing, a Chinese merchant and naturalized citizen, answered the governor in print when the state turned on Chinese miners in 1852. Louise Clappe ('Dame Shirley') saw a camp riot against Spanish speakers and the whippings that followed. William Swain stands for the overland forty-niners who arrived when the easy gold was gone.

Native Californians did much of the early digging: Mason counted them as more than half the miners in 1848, many working for white employers for goods. No firsthand written account by a Native Californian of these years has been found for this chapter. The Pomo record is William Ralganal Benson's narrative, published in 1932 from the testimony of men who took part. It is set beside the official record of Governor Peter Burnett: the statutes of 1850 and his 1851 message expecting a 'war of extermination'. Both are given plainly.

The record is mixed, and the form tags say so. There are true diaries (Bigler, Smith, Colton's published diary, Pérez Rosales), dated letters (Clappe, Swain), newspapers, official reports and statutes, and recollections set down decades later (Sutter's 1857 article, Coronel's 1877 dictation, Benson's 1932 narrative). James Marshall's own later account and Mariano Vallejo's 1875 recollections are not used here. Disputed or legendary moments, such as Brannan's street cry, are marked as such.
calendar_note: All dates are Gregorian and need no conversion. Several key moments are known only from later recollections (Sutter in 1857, Coronel in 1877, Benson in 1932) and carry month or season dates marked approx. Sutter's short diary was probably written up after the fact, and Colton revised his diary for publication in 1850.

eyes.name: Henry William Bigler
eyes.role: Mormon Battalion veteran, aged 32, hired as a labourer on Sutter's sawmill at Coloma
eyes.where: The sawmill site on the South Fork of the American River, Coloma

waypoints.label: Sierra crossing toward Salt Lake, summer 1848

eyes.vantage_label: on the mill crew the day of the find
eyes.authenticity: Two original pages (numbered 176–177) holding the 24 January 1848 entry are held by the Society of California Pioneers, San Francisco. Bigler later wrote fair copies and reminiscences; in 1887 the Society used his diary and Azariah Smith's to fix the discovery date at 24 January. Transcriptions differ slightly, some preserving repeated words in the manuscript.
eyes.bio: A farmer's son from western Virginia who had marched with the Mormon Battalion to California, Bigler was working for wages to earn money to rejoin the Saints in the Great Basin. His one-line entry is the only record written on the day itself, and historians have fixed the date of the discovery by it. He wrote as a worker on the crew, not as an owner.

sources.title: Bigler (Henry William) Diary, 1848 — Society of California Pioneers (OAC finding aid)
Saints and Gold: 1848 (BYU Religious Studies Center)
After Sutter's Mill: The Life of Henry Bigler (Dialogue)

eyes.name: Azariah Smith
eyes.role: Mormon Battalion veteran, aged 21, labourer at the Coloma sawmill
eyes.where: Coloma sawmill, then the nearby diggings
eyes.vantage_label: on the mill crew, homesick and saving wages
eyes.authenticity: Smith's diary survives and was edited by David L. Bigler as The Gold Discovery Journal of Azariah Smith (1990). Because the journal was first published in full long after 1928, it is given here in digest only. In 1887 Smith corresponded with the Society of California Pioneers about the discovery date.
eyes.bio: The youngest of the Battalion men at the mill, Smith kept a plain, often lonely diary of work, weather and Sundays far from his family. He recorded the find a few days after Bigler, with a characteristic hedge that the pieces were only supposed to be gold, and later noted his best day's earnings in the diggings.

sources.title: Bigler and Smith Letters, 1887–1948 — Society of California Pioneers (OAC)
Saints and Gold: 1848 (BYU Religious Studies Center)

eyes.name: John Augustus Sutter (Johann August Suter)
eyes.role: Swiss-born proprietor of New Helvetia (Sutter's Fort), aged 44; owner of the sawmill under construction at Coloma
eyes.side: Mexican land-grantee turned American settler; employer of Native, Hawaiian and Mormon labour
eyes.where: Sutter's Fort on the Sacramento; visits to Coloma
eyes.vantage_label: the owner who could not keep the secret
eyes.authenticity: Sutter's short diary was excerpted in the San Francisco Argonaut in 1878 and published in full as The Diary of Johann August Sutter (Grabhorn Press, 1932); the Virtual Museum of the City of San Francisco notes the entries were probably written up retrospectively. His fuller account, 'The Discovery of Gold in California', appeared in Hutchings' California Magazine in November 1857, nearly ten years after the events.
eyes.bio: Sutter held a Mexican grant of about 50,000 acres in the Sacramento Valley and ran it on the labour of hundreds of Native workers, whom contemporary visitors described as held in conditions close to slavery. The gold rush overran his fort, mills and herds; he spent his last decades petitioning for compensation. His records show the find from the owner's side: tests, secrecy, title and loss.

sources.title: Sutter's diary extracts (The Diary Junction)
John Sutter, 'The Discovery of Gold in California', Hutchings' California Magazine, Nov 1857 (Virtual Museum of the City of San Francisco)

eyes.name: The Californian and the California Star (San Francisco weeklies; Samuel Brannan, proprietor of the Star)
eyes.role: The two English-language weeklies of a town of under a thousand people; Brannan was also a Mormon elder and storekeeper at Sutter's Fort
eyes.vantage_label: the press that first doubted, then spread the news
eyes.authenticity: Issues of both weeklies survive. The first printed notice appeared in the Californian on 15 March 1848. Brannan's street cry of 'Gold! Gold from the American River!' is known from later recollections and histories, not from a contemporary record; sources place it on 10 or 12 May 1848, so it is given as approx.
eyes.bio: Gathered here as one eye because the two small papers are the first public record of the rush and then its first casualty: both suspended within weeks as printers and readers left for the mines. Brannan, who had a store at Sutter's Fort, both advertised the gold region in the Star and stood to profit from selling goods to miners.

sources.title: 'Gold Mine Found', the Californian, 15 March 1848 (Gold Fields Books)
Gary Kamiya, 'Gold Rush stopped the S.F. press as editors fled' (San Francisco Chronicle)
Saints and Gold: 1848 (BYU Religious Studies Center)

eyes.name: Walter Colton
eyes.role: US Navy chaplain, aged 50, serving as alcalde (magistrate) of Monterey under the military government
eyes.where: Monterey; the southern mines on the Stanislaus and Tuolumne, autumn 1848
eyes.vantage_label: the magistrate of the capital watching it empty
eyes.authenticity: Published as Three Years in California (New York, 1850) in dated diary form; Colton revised his entries for the press, so the wording is his published text rather than an untouched manuscript.
eyes.bio: A Vermont-born clergyman and journalist who had co-founded the Californian in 1846, Colton recorded the slow arrival of belief in Monterey: rumour, doubt, a messenger, then the flight of servants, soldiers and tradesmen. He then went to the mines himself, and his figures for yields and numbers are among the earliest outside estimates.

sources.title: Walter Colton, The Land of Gold; or, Three Years in California (Project Gutenberg)

eyes.name: Colonel Richard Barnes Mason
eyes.role: US Army colonel, 1st Dragoons; military governor of California, aged 51; accompanied by Lt. William T. Sherman
eyes.where: Monterey; inspection tour of the mines, July 1848
eyes.vantage_label: the governor who went to see for himself
eyes.authenticity: Mason's report to the Adjutant-General, dated Headquarters, Monterey, 17 August 1848, was printed with the President's message of December 1848 and is a US-government record. Sherman, who drafted much of Mason's correspondence, described the tour in his Memoirs (1875), written later.
eyes.bio: Mason governed a conquered province whose status was still unsettled when the gold was found. His report, with its measured figures and its count of Indian miners, turned rumour into an official finding in Washington, and his reply to Sutter's request for title to the mill site showed that the land question would not be easily settled.

sources.title: Col. R. B. Mason, report of 17 August 1848 (Virtual Museum of the City of San Francisco)
W. T. Sherman, Memoirs, ch. II extract (California Military Museum)

eyes.name: James Knox Polk
eyes.role: Eleventh President of the United States, aged 53, in the last months of his term
eyes.authenticity: Fourth Annual Message to Congress, 5 December 1848; US-government record, transcribed by the American Presidency Project and the Miller Center.
eyes.bio: Polk had led the war that brought California under US control. His message, citing reports of officers who had seen the mines, gave the news the stamp of the federal government and set off the mass migration of 1849.

sources.title: Fourth Annual Message, 5 December 1848 (American Presidency Project)
Miller Center transcript

eyes.name: Antonio Franco Coronel
eyes.role: Californio of Los Angeles, about 31 in 1848; schoolteacher and minor official; later mayor of Los Angeles and state treasurer
eyes.where: Los Angeles; the northern diggings (Placer Seco, the American and Stanislaus rivers), 1848–49
eyes.vantage_label: a Californio miner driven from the diggings
eyes.authenticity: 'Cosas de California' was dictated in Spanish to Thomas Savage for H. H. Bancroft's history project in 1877, nearly thirty years after the events; the manuscript is in the Bancroft Library. It is available in English in David J. and Carol S. Weber's translation (Tales of Mexican California, 1994). No quotation from the modern translation is given.
eyes.bio: Coronel led a party of Angelenos, including Native servants, north to the mines in 1848 and did well. Returning in March 1849, he found the diggings crowded, divided by nationality and ruled by force, and he recorded the notices and armed gatherings that drove Spanish-speaking miners off their claims. His is the fullest Californio account of the diggings.

sources.title: 'Antonio Franco Coronel Describes Tensions Among Miners' (HERB, American Social History Project)
Antonio Franco Coronel (PBS American Experience: The Gold Rush)
Documentos para la historia de California [Coronel] (OAC)

eyes.name: Vicente Pérez Rosales
eyes.role: Chilean farmer and entrepreneur, aged 41, who sailed to California with his brothers
eyes.where: Valparaíso; San Francisco; Sacramento and Coloma diggings
eyes.vantage_label: a foreign miner from the south
eyes.authenticity: His Diario de un viaje a California (1848–1849) survives and is published in Chile (Memoria Chilena holds it); he later reworked the material into his memoir Recuerdos del pasado. Given in digest only; no quotation from translation.
eyes.bio: Pérez Rosales was one of thousands of Chileans who reached California early, because news travelled fast along the Pacific trade routes. His record shows the rush from the side of Spanish-speaking foreigners: early success, hostility from American miners, a refusal to join a raid on Native people, and retreat into trade in San Francisco.

sources.title: Diario de un viaje a California (1848–1849) (Memoria Chilena)
Vicente Pérez Rosales (PBS American Experience: The Gold Rush)

eyes.name: William Swain
eyes.role: Farmer from Youngstown, New York, aged 27, who left his wife, infant daughter and brother to go overland
eyes.where: The California Trail; the Feather River diggings
eyes.authenticity: Swain's diary and his family's letters, held at Yale's Beinecke Library, were published by J. S. Holliday in The World Rushed In (1981). Because they were first published after 1928, they are given in digest only. Dates here are approximate.
eyes.bio: Swain was one of the tens of thousands drawn west by the reports confirmed in Washington in December 1848. His letters home, and his brother's and wife's letters to him, show the rush from a farm household: the hope, the long crossing, disappointing returns, and the pull to come home.

sources.title: J. S. Holliday, The World Rushed In: The California Gold Rush Experience (1981)

eyes.name: Louise Amelia Knapp Smith Clappe ('Dame Shirley')
eyes.role: New England-born writer, aged 32, wife of a doctor practising at the Feather River camps
eyes.where: Rich Bar and Indian Bar, East Branch of the North Fork of the Feather River
eyes.vantage_label: a woman in a mining camp, writing letters
eyes.authenticity: Twenty-three letters to her sister, dated September 1851 to November 1852, were published in The Pioneer (San Francisco) in 1854–55 and collected as The Shirley Letters; the published texts are her own revisions of the letters.
eyes.bio: Clappe wrote with wit and a sharp eye about the camps' daily life, their brief prosperity and their violence. Her letters of July and August 1852 record a Fourth of July riot against 'Spaniards' and a vigilance committee's whippings and expulsions, with her own horror plainly stated.

sources.title: The Shirley Letters from California Mines in 1851–52 (Project Gutenberg)

eyes.name: Norman Asing (Yuan Sheng)
eyes.role: Chinese merchant and restaurant owner in San Francisco, a naturalized American citizen
eyes.vantage_label: a Chinese merchant answering the governor
eyes.authenticity: Published in the Daily Alta California, 5 May 1852, as a reply to Governor John Bigler's message calling for restriction of Chinese immigration; widely reprinted in documentary collections.
eyes.bio: Asing had lived in the United States, by his own account, for years before the rush, and in 1852 he was a leader among San Francisco's Chinese merchants. His letter is one of very few public statements in English by a Chinese Californian of the gold-rush years, written as the state moved to tax and exclude Chinese miners.

sources.title: 'To His Excellency Governor Bigler' (History Matters, George Mason University)
Norman Asing petition (National Constitution Center)

eyes.name: William Ralganal Benson
eyes.role: Pomo (Eastern Pomo) man of Clear Lake, hereditary chief, interpreter and author; not an eyewitness
eyes.vantage_label: the people whose land and labour were taken, in their own account
eyes.authenticity: 'The Stone and Kelsey "Massacre" on the Shores of Clear Lake in 1849: The Indian Viewpoint', California Historical Society Quarterly 11:3 (September 1932), pp. 266–273, introduced by Max Radin. Benson wrote down what five Pomo men who took part had told him; Radin noted he was not an eyewitness and the account could contain distortions. First published after 1928, so digest only.
eyes.bio: No surviving firsthand written account by a Native Californian of 1848–50 has been found for this chapter. Benson's narrative, set down from the testimony of participants, is the Pomo record of forced herding labour under two ranchers who had also taken Clear Lake men to the diggings, of the killing of those ranchers, and of the army's attack that followed.

sources.title: W. R. Benson, 'The Stone and Kelsey Massacre…', CHSQ 1932 (PDF, California Military Museum)

eyes.name: Peter Hardeman Burnett
eyes.role: First civilian governor of the State of California (Dec 1849–Jan 1851), aged 42; former Oregon settler and gold-rush miner
eyes.where: San Jose, the first state capital
eyes.vantage_label: the governor, by statute and message
eyes.authenticity: Burnett's annual message of 6 January 1851 is printed in the Journal of the Senate and held by the California State Library's governors' addresses collection. The 1850 statutes are official records of the first legislature.
eyes.bio: Burnett had come down from Oregon in 1848 and tried the diggings himself before entering politics. As governor he presided over the first state laws on foreign miners and on Native Californians, and his 1851 message spoke openly of a war of extermination as something to be expected. The official record is given plainly, as written.

sources.title: Peter Burnett, address of 6 January 1851 (California State Library, Governors' Gallery)
Foreign Miners' Tax Act of 1850 (Wikipedia)
Act for the Government and Protection of Indians (Wikiwand)

entries.headline: A Sunday of homesickness at the half-built mill
entries.digest: Five weeks before the find, Smith wrote of a mill camp in the hills where Sundays were the hardest days. Home kept running in his mind and he felt lonely. The crew of Battalion veterans was working for wages to buy their way back to their families and the Saints.
entries.source_note: Azariah Smith journal, 19 Dec 1847, as quoted in BYU RSC 'Saints and Gold: 1848'.

entries.headline: Pomo men herded and hungry under Stone and Kelsey
entries.digest: Benson's narrative, set down from the testimony of Pomo men, describes two ranchers who had taken over the Clear Lake country making Pomo men herd their cattle, horses and hogs for little food, while hunger spread through the villages. Punishments were harsh and people were confined after dark. Max Radin's introduction adds that Clear Lake men were taken on one rancher's 1848 expedition to the diggings almost as slaves, and few returned.
entries.source_note: Benson, CHSQ 11:3 (1932), pp. 266–273, with Radin's introduction; the 1848 diggings trip is in Radin's introduction, not Benson's text.

entries.headline: Metal like gold turns up in the tail race
entries.digest: In a single line between notes of the day's work, Bigler recorded that some kind of metal had been found in the mill's tail race and that it looked like gold. He spelled it as he spoke it and credited no one by name in this line. He did not know he was writing the founding date of the gold rush; later historians fixed the day by this entry.
entries.quote: some kind of mettle … looks like goald
entries.source_note: Society of California Pioneers, Bigler diary pp. 176–177 (OAC C059079); text as in BYU RSC 'Saints and Gold: 1848'.

entries.headline: Marshall rides in through heavy rain
entries.digest: Sutter's diary notes that Marshall arrived in the evening in heavy rain, saying he had come on important business. The entry gives no hint of what the business was. Sutter's short diary was probably written up later, so even this terse line is not strictly a same-day record.
entries.source_note: Sutter diary, 28 Jan 1848 (Diary of Johann August Sutter, 1932; extracts via The Diary Junction).

entries.headline: Aqua fortis and the encyclopedia: Sutter tests the metal
entries.digest: Writing nearly ten years later, Sutter recalled Marshall arriving agitated and insisting on privacy. Together they tried about two ounces of the metal with aqua fortis from the fort's apothecary and compared it with the entry for gold in the Encyclopedia Americana, and Sutter judged it gold of the finest quality. Sutter's later account dates the find to early January, not the 24th.
entries.source_note: Sutter, 'The Discovery of Gold in California', Hutchings' California Magazine, Nov 1857 (SF Museum transcription). Day taken from the diary entry above.

entries.headline: A cautious note: pieces of supposed gold
entries.digest: On the following Sunday Smith noted that during the week Marshall had found some pieces of what the crew all supposed to be gold. His wording hedges the identification. He went back to millwork and, like the others, began to look for gold on his free days.
entries.source_note: Gold Discovery Journal of Azariah Smith (ed. D. L. Bigler, 1990); day widely cited but not checked against the edition for this chapter.

entries.headline: Sutter rides up to the sawmill
entries.digest: Sutter recorded leaving for the sawmill with a vaquero named Olimpio and being away from the 2nd to the 5th. In his 1857 account he says he asked the mill hands to keep the find secret for six weeks so he could finish his flour mill. The secret lasted far less.
entries.quote: keep this discovery secret only for six weeks
entries.source_note: Sutter diary, 1 Feb 1848; quote from Hutchings' Nov 1857 account (SF Museum).

entries.headline: The first Mormon crews leave to dig
entries.digest: Sutter noted that the first party of Mormons he employed left to wash and dig for gold, and that very soon all followed. Days earlier, on 2 March, two Battalion men had made a rich strike at the place soon called Mormon Island. His workforce, the basis of his enterprises, was beginning to dissolve.
entries.source_note: Sutter diary, 7 Mar 1848 (Diary Junction extracts); Mormon Island date from BYU RSC.

entries.headline: First printed notice: 'Gold Mine Found'
entries.digest: The Californian ran a short item reporting that gold had been found in the race of the new sawmill on the American Fork. It suggested California was rich in minerals and offered an opening for 'scientific capitalists'. The item drew little reaction in a town that had heard mineral rumours before.
entries.quote: gold has been found in considerable quantities
entries.source_note: The Californian, 15 Mar 1848 (Gold Fields Books transcription); CGS 'The Discovery of Gold in California'.

entries.headline: Brannan's Star prints the gold country for the East
entries.digest: Sam Brannan's California Star issued a special edition promoting California for readers in the eastern states, noting a mine of gold whose size could not yet be estimated. Copies went east two days later with a pack train that included Mormon Battalion men. The aim was to attract settlers as much as to report a strike.
entries.quote: It has a mine of gold
entries.source_note: California Star, 1 Apr 1848, as quoted in BYU RSC 'Saints and Gold: 1848'.

entries.headline: The Star's editor visits the mill and calls it a sham
entries.digest: Edward Kemble, running the Star, went up to Coloma and came back unconvinced, telling readers the reports were a sham. Within weeks events overtook him. The episode is known from later histories that reproduce his words.
entries.source_note: Kamiya, San Francisco Chronicle, citing secondary histories; date of Kemble's visit not fixed.

entries.headline: Brannan's bottle of dust on Montgomery Street
entries.digest: By later accounts, Brannan came down from Sutter's Fort, where he kept a store, and walked through San Francisco holding up a bottle of gold dust and shouting that it came from the American River. Whatever the exact words, the town began to empty within days. Brannan stood to sell picks, pans and provisions to every man who left.
entries.source_note: BYU RSC (10 May meeting, cry soon after); Kamiya, SF Chronicle (12 May). The cry is recorded in later recollections, not in a contemporary document.

entries.headline: The great rush from San Francisco reaches the fort
entries.digest: Sutter recorded the great rush from San Francisco arriving at the fort, with friends and acquaintances filling every house. Two days later a man opened the first hotel in the fort's large building and, Sutter noted, made a great deal of money. His fort had become a way station for other men's fortunes.
entries.source_note: Sutter diary, 19 and 21 May 1848 (Diary Junction extracts).

entries.headline: The Californian stops the presses
entries.digest: The Californian ceased publication because its staff and readers had gone to the gold fields. About two weeks later the Star also announced that it had expired. San Francisco briefly had no newspaper at all.
entries.source_note: Kamiya, SF Chronicle: Californian suspended 29 May 1848; Star's end about two weeks later (approx).

entries.headline: The first rumour reaches the capital
entries.digest: Colton recorded the first report in Monterey that gold had been found on the American Fork. People talked and wondered but mostly disbelieved it. The same day the Californian, which he had helped found, was folding in San Francisco.
entries.quote: gold had been discovered on the American Fork
entries.source_note: Colton, Three Years in California (1850), ch. XVIII, entry of 29 May 1848 (Project Gutenberg).

entries.headline: The alcalde sends a messenger to find out
entries.digest: After a second report of gold turned up while digging a mill race, Colton sent a man on a round trip of some four hundred miles to the American Fork to bring back the truth. It was the cautious act of a magistrate who did not want to be fooled. A week later a straggler arrived with an ounce of yellow ore that some still called a hoax.
entries.quote: dispatched a messenger this morning to the American Fork
entries.source_note: Colton, entries of 5, 6 and 12 June 1848 (Project Gutenberg).

entries.headline: The messenger returns, and the town leaves
entries.digest: Colton's messenger came back with specimens and the doubters gave way. Tradesmen dropped their work and set off for the mines, and Colton described a capital left with hardly anyone but women and a few officials. He could no longer find men to keep order.
entries.quote: All were off for the mines
entries.source_note: Colton, entry of 20 June 1848 (Project Gutenberg).

entries.headline: Sixty-five dollars on his best day
entries.digest: Smith recorded men, women and children from the Bay and elsewhere flocking to the gold mine. He noted that the most he made in one day was sixty-five dollars after the toll was taken out. Like most of the Battalion men, he used his gold to go home to the Saints rather than stay.
entries.source_note: Azariah Smith journal, as quoted (undated) in BYU RSC 'Saints and Gold: 1848'.

entries.headline: The mill crew leaves the gold for Salt Lake
entries.digest: With their wages and dust, Bigler and other Battalion veterans left the gold country in the summer of 1848 and crossed the Sierra toward the Great Basin, opening a wagon route over the mountains. They chose rejoining their families and their church over the richest diggings in the world. Bigler kept his diary on the way.
entries.source_note: Dialogue, 'After Sutter's Mill: The Life of Henry Bigler, 1848–1900'; exact dates not checked for this chapter.

entries.headline: The governor sees two hundred men at the Lower Mines
entries.digest: After the Fourth of July at Sutter's Fort, Mason and Sherman rode about twenty-five miles to the Mormon Diggings. Mason counted about two hundred men working with pans and rough cradles and noted that one party of four was averaging a hundred dollars a day. He then went on to Coloma and the side ravines.
entries.source_note: Mason report, 17 Aug 1848 (SF Museum); Sherman, Memoirs ch. II (California Military Museum).

entries.headline: Every servant in Monterey has gone
entries.digest: Colton noted that servants were quitting across town, and that he and other officers now cooked for themselves. Three days later a sailor came in with a bag holding 136 ounces of gold, and more carpenters and soldiers left. Deserting soldiers worried the officers of the military government.
entries.quote: The gold fever has reached every servant in Monterey
entries.source_note: Colton, entries of 15 and 18 July 1848 (Project Gutenberg).

entries.place: Northern diggings (Placer Seco and the American River)
entries.headline: A Californio party strikes it rich
entries.digest: Coronel recalled reaching the diggings with a party of Angelenos and their Native servants and doing very well. He remembered the first three days' takings as 45, 38 and 51 ounces, and a blanket traded for nine ounces. In 1848 the diggings were still thinly peopled and Californios, Sonorans and Americans worked side by side.
entries.source_note: Coronel, 'Cosas de California' (dictated 1877), as summarised by PBS American Experience and HERB. Figures are his later recollection.

entries.headline: Four townsmen come home with $76,844
entries.digest: Colton recorded four Monterey men returning from the mines with gold dust worth about $76,844, and listed other individual yields to show the scale. He treated the figures as news to be set down rather than verified. The next day the governor signed his report to Washington.
entries.quote: seventy-six thousand eight hundred and forty-four dollars
entries.source_note: Colton, entry of 16 Aug 1848 (Project Gutenberg).

entries.headline: Report to Washington: more gold than the war cost
entries.digest: Mason estimated that upwards of four thousand men were working the gold district, more than half of them Indians, and that the region yielded thirty to fifty thousand dollars a day. He named employers who had thirty, fifty and about a hundred Indians digging for them, some paid in goods. He concluded that the gold of the Sacramento and San Joaquin country would pay the cost of the war with Mexico many times over.
entries.quote: will pay the cost of the present war
entries.source_note: Mason to Adjutant-General R. Jones, 17 Aug 1848 (SF Museum transcription).

entries.headline: In the diggings, less than half an ounce a day
entries.digest: Colton had left Monterey on 21 September and now worked and watched in the southern diggings. He judged that the average digger made less than half an ounce a day, because men wasted time chasing rumours of richer ground. The next day a rumour of a solid pocket on the Stanislaus emptied the camp, and the diggers came back disappointed.
entries.source_note: Colton, entries of 21 Sept, 18 and 19 Oct 1848 (Project Gutenberg).

entries.headline: Some fifty thousand people on the slopes
entries.digest: Colton estimated that some fifty thousand people were now roaming the Sierra foothills in search of gold, a figure that was a guess rather than a count. Rum in the camp cost twenty dollars a quart. He started home a few days later and was back in Monterey on 2 December.
entries.source_note: Colton, entries of 2 and 8 Nov and 2 Dec 1848 (Project Gutenberg).

entries.headline: The President confirms the gold
entries.digest: In his last annual message Polk told Congress that the accounts of gold in California would be hard to believe if officers who had visited the district had not confirmed them. He cited the commanding officer's July visit and about four thousand miners, and described a country where nearly the whole male population had left for the diggings and soldiers were deserting. Mason's report was laid before Congress with the message.
entries.source_note: Polk, Fourth Annual Message, 5 Dec 1848 (American Presidency Project; Bedford excerpt).

entries.headline: Chilean brothers sail north
entries.digest: Pérez Rosales and his brothers sailed for California after Chilean ships came back that autumn with California gold. News had reached Chile months before most of the eastern United States took it seriously. The voyage north took about six weeks.
entries.source_note: PBS American Experience profile drawing on his diary; Memoria Chilena, Diario de un viaje a California.

entries.headline: Arrival in a harbour of abandoned ships
entries.digest: Pérez Rosales reached San Francisco and went on by boat to Sacramento and then to Coloma. There he and his brothers worked a cradle and, for a while, did very well. He found that it paid at times to pass as a Frenchman rather than a Chilean.
entries.source_note: PBS American Experience profile; arrival date given there.

entries.headline: Back in the mines: notices against foreigners
entries.digest: Returning for a second season, Coronel found the diggings crowded and camps divided by nationality. Notices appeared giving all 'foreigners' twenty-four hours to leave, and armed groups gathered on a hill in a standoff that lasted several days. He explained the resentment as envy of skilled Sonoran miners by later arrivals who found little, and said force was the only law.
entries.source_note: Coronel, 'Cosas de California' (1877), HERB excerpt (Weber translation) and PBS profile; no exact date given.

entries.place: San Francisco and the Sacramento diggings
entries.headline: Chilean camps raided; the brothers give up mining
entries.digest: Pérez Rosales heard in San Francisco of attacks on Chileans near his brothers' camp and paid two hundred dollars for a boat back up the river. He found his brothers robbed but unhurt, and they gave up mining for trade. In the same season he refused an invitation from American miners to join an attack on a Native village, and recorded with horror the captives they brought back.
entries.source_note: PBS American Experience profile drawing on his diary; the raid on the village is undated there.

entries.headline: Driven off his claim, Coronel rides home
entries.digest: Coronel recalled following American miners who set out to attack a Native village they blamed for killing two Americans, and witnessing people shot as they fled. On the American River about a hundred armed Americans then took over his own claim. He gave up and rode home to Los Angeles.
entries.source_note: PBS American Experience profile of Coronel's 'Cosas de California'; no exact dates in the account.

entries.headline: A farmer leaves wife, baby and brother for the gold
entries.digest: Swain set out from his farm on the Niagara frontier for the Missouri jumping-off towns, leaving his wife Sabrina, their infant daughter and his brother George to run the farm. He joined a company of Michigan men for the overland crossing. His diary and letters home start here.
entries.source_note: Holliday, The World Rushed In (1981); exact departure day not checked for this chapter.

entries.headline: The ranchers are killed
entries.digest: Benson recorded that after a dispute over horses and long mistreatment, a group of Pomo men resolved to act and killed Stone and Kelsey at their house. He named the five men whose account he wrote down. The narrative presents the killing as the response of people pushed beyond endurance.
entries.source_note: Benson, CHSQ 1932; Radin dates the killings to autumn 1849.

entries.headline: Reaching the mines after the long crossing
entries.digest: After months on the trail and the hard Lassen route, Swain reached the northern diggings as the rainy season began. He found the easy gold already worked and the returns far below what the reports had promised. His letters home weighed staying against the cost of failure.
entries.source_note: Holliday, The World Rushed In (1981); dates approximate.

entries.headline: A $20 monthly tax on foreign miners
entries.digest: The legislature's Foreign Miners' Tax Act, signed by Governor Burnett, charged foreign miners twenty dollars a month for the right to dig. It fell hardest on Mexicans, Chileans, Peruvians and other Spanish-speaking miners; Native Californians were specifically exempted. On 19 May some four thousand mostly Mexican and Peruvian miners protested at Sonora and were dispersed by an armed force.
entries.source_note: Foreign Miners' Tax Act of 1850 (Wikipedia summary of the statute); repealed 1851.

entries.headline: The Act for the Government and Protection of Indians
entries.digest: Under Burnett the legislature passed Chapter 133 of the statutes of 1850. It let settlers take custody of Native children as 'apprentices' until 18 for boys and 15 for girls, allowed Native people found 'loitering' to be arrested and hired out to the highest bidder, and barred convicting a white person on an Indian's testimony. It was later widened in 1860, and its indenture provisions were abolished in 1863.
entries.source_note: Act for the Government and Protection of Indians (Wikiwand summary of Cal. Stats. 1850 ch. 133).

entries.place: Clear Lake, island near Emerson Hill
entries.headline: Soldiers attack the island camp
entries.digest: Benson's narrative describes soldiers coming across Clear Lake by boat and attacking a Pomo camp on an island, killing many people. The account is told soberly, from the survivors' side. The attack is known in history as the Bloody Island massacre.
entries.source_note: Benson, CHSQ 1932 (no month given); 15 May 1850 is the date given in military and secondary sources.

entries.headline: The governor's message: a war of extermination
entries.digest: In his annual message Burnett told the legislature that a war of extermination would continue between the two races until the Indian race became extinct, and that this must be expected. He blamed treaty failures, settlers' seizure of land without payment, and hunger driving Native people to take livestock. He described the outcome as beyond human power to prevent and said he regarded it with regret.
entries.quote: war of extermination will continue to be waged
entries.source_note: Burnett, address of 6 Jan 1851 (California State Library governors' addresses).

entries.headline: A triumphant entry into Rich Bar
entries.digest: Clappe's first letter describes a hard mule journey into the canyon and her arrival at a camp of rough cabins and tents, where she lodged at the grandly named Empire Hotel. She wrote as an amused outsider, counting very few women. The camp was barely a year old.
entries.source_note: Shirley Letters, Letter the First, Rich Bar, 13 Sept 1851 (Project Gutenberg).

entries.headline: The governor calls for curbing Chinese immigration
entries.digest: Governor John Bigler sent the legislature a message urging measures to check Chinese immigration, describing Chinese miners as unwanted contract labourers. Within days the legislature passed a new foreign miners' licence tax of three dollars a month that fell mainly on Chinese miners. Asing read the message as an attack on his community and on himself as a citizen.
entries.source_note: History Matters introduction to Asing's letter; 1852 licence tax rate from Foreign Miners' Tax Act article; exact dates not checked.

entries.headline: A naturalized Chinese citizen answers the governor
entries.digest: Asing published an open letter to Governor Bigler, declaring himself a naturalized citizen and a republican who loved free institutions. He argued that Chinese people had brought commerce and industry and were not the degraded race the governor described.
entries.quote: we are not the degraded race you would make us
entries.source_note: Daily Alta California, 5 May 1852 (History Matters, GMU).

entries.headline: Native visitors at the cabin door
entries.digest: Clappe described Native people who came to the camp, their huts, food and dress, with an outsider's curiosity and the condescension common to her time. Her letter shows Native people living at the edges of a camp built on their river. It records nothing in their own words.
entries.source_note: Shirley Letters, Letter the Seventeenth, Indian Bar, 25 May 1852 (Project Gutenberg).

entries.headline: A Fourth of July riot against the 'Spaniards'
entries.digest: Writing the day after Independence Day, Clappe described the celebration turning into a fight around five in the afternoon, with Americans shouting against the Spanish-speaking miners and several men badly wounded. 'Spaniards' in the camps meant Mexicans, Chileans and other Spanish speakers. She was frightened and plainly disapproving.
entries.source_note: Shirley Letters, Letter the Eighteenth, Indian Bar, 5 July 1852 (Project Gutenberg).

entries.headline: Whippings and expulsion after a stabbing
entries.digest: Clappe recounted how, on Sunday 11 July, a Spanish-speaking man named Domingo stabbed an American, Tom Somers, who died within minutes. A vigilance committee tried the Spanish speakers in camp, sentenced two to be whipped and ordered others, including a Mexican woman, to leave. She wrote of her anguish at hearing the blows.
entries.quote: imagine my anguish when I heard the first blow fall
entries.source_note: Shirley Letters, Letter the Nineteenth, Indian Bar, 4 Aug 1852 (Project Gutenberg).

entries.headline: Ten years on: 'a great misfortune' for Sutter
entries.digest: In his magazine account Sutter listed what the gold had cost him: workers who left from the clerk to the cook, millstones stolen, a tannery abandoned, herds and lands overrun by squatters. He blamed the courts and the Land Commission for the slow fate of his grant. It is a claim of loss by a man whose own enterprise had rested on Native labour.
entries.quote: What a great misfortune was this sudden gold discovery for me!
entries.source_note: Sutter, Hutchings' California Magazine, Nov 1857 (SF Museum transcription).

convergences.label: The find at Coloma, and the week after
convergences.note: The worker wrote one line on the day; the owner recorded only that Marshall rode in on 'important business' four days later, and recalled the tests in detail ten years on; the youngest crewman hedged that the pieces were only supposed to be gold.

convergences.label: Word leaks: crews leave and the first notice is printed
convergences.note: Sutter watched his Mormon hands leave to dig on 7 March; a week later the Californian printed the news to general indifference.

convergences.label: San Francisco empties
convergences.note: Brannan's bottle of dust, the rush arriving at Sutter's Fort on 19 May, the Californian's suspension on 29 May and the first rumour in Monterey the same day: the same weeks seen from the press, the owner and the capital.

convergences.label: The governor at the diggings; Monterey without servants
convergences.note: Mason counted two hundred men at Mormon Island while Colton, his alcalde, cooked his own meals in an emptied capital and the mill crew took their best days' earnings.

convergences.label: Figures go to Washington
convergences.note: Colton's $76,844 and Mason's thirty to fifty thousand dollars a day were set down within a day of each other; Coronel's recalled ounces show the same season from a Californio claim. Only Mason counted the Indian miners who made up more than half the workforce.

convergences.label: The news goes official and goes abroad
convergences.note: Polk confirmed the gold to Congress on 5 December; three weeks later Chileans who had heard months earlier were already sailing north.

convergences.label: Spanish speakers driven from the diggings
convergences.note: A Californio and a Chilean, from different countries but both counted as 'foreigners', recorded notices, raids and seized claims in the same spring; each also recorded American attacks on Native villages.

convergences.label: The first state laws: foreigners taxed, Native people bound
convergences.note: Within nine days the legislature taxed foreign miners and passed the indenture act; within a month soldiers attacked the Pomo at Clear Lake. The official record and the Pomo record describe the same spring from opposite sides.

convergences.label: 1852: the camps and the capital turn on outsiders
convergences.note: Asing answered the governor in print in May; Clappe recorded the riot and whippings of Spanish speakers at Indian Bar in July. Both record the line drawn between citizen and foreigner, one from inside the targeted group, one as a horrified bystander.

ties.note: Both worked on the Coloma mill crew and kept diaries of the same days; in 1887 both were consulted by the Society of California Pioneers to fix the discovery date.
Bigler was a wage labourer at Sutter's sawmill; Sutter was his employer.
Smith also worked for wages on Sutter's mill, and his crew's departure to dig is what Sutter recorded on 7 March 1848.
Brannan kept a store at Sutter's Fort and learned of the gold through the Mormon workers there before announcing it in San Francisco.
Brannan was the leading Mormon elder in California, and Battalion veterans carried his Star's special edition east in April 1848.
Colton co-founded the Californian at Monterey in 1846; the paper that printed the first gold notice was his own creation, later moved to San Francisco.
Colton served as alcalde of Monterey under Mason's military government; both wrote of the same emptying capital in summer 1848.
Mason and Sherman spent the Fourth of July 1848 at Sutter's Fort; earlier Mason had declined to promise Sutter title to the Coloma mill site.
Mason's report of 17 August 1848 was the officer's account Polk cited and laid before Congress on 5 December.
The President's confirmation of the gold, reprinted across the eastern press that winter, set off the overland migration Swain joined in April 1849.
A Californio and a Chilean in the northern diggings in spring 1849, both driven off claims as 'foreigners' by American miners.

Burnett signed the 1850 foreign miners' tax that fell on Spanish-speaking miners such as those Coronel had led; Californios were nominally citizens under the 1848 treaty but were often treated as foreigners in the diggings.
The governor's 1850 statutes and 1851 message, and the Pomo account of the same years at Clear Lake.
The 'Spaniards' driven from Indian Bar in 1852 were the same Spanish-speaking miners whose expulsion Coronel had recorded in 1849.

A sailor brings 136 ounces of gold into Monterey

threads_out.note: The Klondike stampede of 1897–98 drew on veterans and folk memory of California; Seattle and San Francisco newspapers sold the new rush as another 1849, and the placer methods (pan, rocker, sluice) came north from the California diggings.

Both rushes rested on the labour of Indigenous people: the Andean mita at Potosí, and the Native Californians whom Mason counted as more than half of the miners in 1848 and whom the 1850 act bound by indenture.
California miners, engineers and methods carried the gold-rush pattern to Australia in 1851 and later to South Africa, where several American mining engineers worked the Witwatersrand reefs.
The California and later gold rushes enlarged the world's gold supply and helped carry the major economies onto the gold standard that the United States finally abandoned in 1971.

California's admission as a free state in 1850, a direct result of the rush's population boom, was part of the Compromise of 1850 that delayed but did not prevent the sectional war; Sherman, who toured the mines with Mason, became one of its leading generals.
